summary.text: Assuming the identities, the shifted terms \(a_n+1\) satisfy the Fibonacci recurrence; a finite computation through index \(3774\) and matrix exponentiation modulo \(p=195318521017\) show that \(p\) divides both \(a_{249580077007}\) and \(a_{249580077006}\). Thus their gcd is at least \(2\), so at \(n=249580077008\) the defining value \(g+(x+y)/g\) is strictly less than \(1+x+y\), contradicting the first claimed identity.

full_proof.text:
Let \((a_n)_{n\geq 1}\) be the sequence defined by
\[
a_1=a_2=1,
\qquad
a_n=g_n+\frac{a_{n-1}+a_{n-2}}{g_n}\quad(n\geq3),
\qquad
g_n=\gcd(a_{n-1},a_{n-2}).
\]
We will show that the first of the three asserted formulas cannot hold for every \(n\geq3775\). Since the conjecture asserts all three formulas simultaneously, this suffices to disprove the entire conjecture.

Set
\[
p=195318521017,
\qquad K=249580073233,
\qquad N=K+3775=249580077008.
\]
The argument is by contradiction. Assume that the conjecture holds. In particular, assume
\[
a_n=1+a_{n-1}+a_{n-2} \tag{1}
\]
for every \(n\geq3775\).

We first record the finite initial calculation needed to start a modular recurrence. Direct iteration of the defining gcd recurrence from \(a_1=a_2=1\) through index 3774 gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{3773}={}&,\\[2mm]
a_{3774}={}&.
\end{aligned} \tag{2}
\]
This is an ordinary finite calculation: begin with the ordered pair \((r,s)=(1,1)\), and for each \(n=3,4,\ldots,3774\), compute
\[
g=\gcd(r,s),\qquad t=g+\frac{r+s}{g},
\]
then replace \((r,s)\) by \((s,t)\). After the 3772 updates the resulting ordered pair is exactly the pair displayed in (2). Thus every update is precisely one application of the defining recurrence, and the final pair is \((a_{3773},a_{3774})\).

Reducing the two displayed integers modulo \(p\) gives
\[
a_{3773}+1\equiv77940394259\pmod p,
\qquad
a_{3774}+1\equiv99768150822\pmod p. \tag{3}
\]
These reductions are just integer divisions of the numbers in (2) by \(195318521017\).

The reason for shifting the sequence by 1 is that (1) then becomes the homogeneous Fibonacci recurrence. Define, for \(i\geq0\),
\[
b_i\equiv a_{3773+i}+1\pmod p.
\]
For every \(i\geq0\), applying (1) at \(n=3775+i\) gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{3775+i}+1
 &=2+a_{3774+i}+a_{3773+i}\\
 &=(a_{3774+i}+1)+(a_{3773+i}+1).
\end{aligned}
\]
Consequently
\[
b_{i+2}=b_{i+1}+b_i\quad\text{in }\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z. \tag{4}
\]
In particular, if
\[
M=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix},
\]
then (4) says
\[
\binom{b_{i+1}}{b_i}=M^i\binom{b_1}{b_0}. \tag{5}
\]
By (3), the initial vector in (5) is
\[
\binom{b_1}{b_0}
= inom{99768150822}{77940394259}
\quad\text{in }(\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z)^2. \tag{6}
\]

We next give the modular exponentiation calculation that locates the failure. Repeated squaring modulo \(p\) yields
\[
M^K=M^{249580073233}
\equiv
\begin{pmatrix}
139205883321&21827756563\\
21827756563&117378126758
\end{pmatrix}
\pmod p. \tag{7}
\]
For completeness, this calculation can be reproduced without handling any enormous Fibonacci integer as follows. Starting with \(M^0=I\), use the exponent chain
\[
\begin{gathered}
0,1,3,7,14,29,58,116,232,464,929,1859,3719,7438,14876,29752,59504,119009,238018,476036,952072,1904144,3808289,7616579,15233158,30466317,60932635,121865270,243730540,487461080,974922161,1949844322,3899688644,7799377288,15598754577,31197509154,62395018308,124790036616,249580073233.
\end{gathered}
\]

Here the four entries on a row are the entries of \(M^e\), read row by row. This table establishes (7) solely through modular matrix multiplication.

Multiplying the last matrix in (7) by the vector in (6), before reduction modulo \(p\), gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
139205883321\cdot99768150822
 +21827756563\cdot77940394259
 &=15589577514788957011679\\
 &=1+195318521017\cdot79816176334,
\end{aligned}
\]
and
\[
\begin{aligned}
21827756563\cdot99768150822
 +117378126758\cdot77940394259
 &=11326212385784681827108\\
 &=1+195318521017\cdot57988419771.
\end{aligned}
\]
Therefore (5) at \(i=K\) gives
\[
(b_{K+1},b_K)\equiv(1,1)\pmod p. \tag{8}
\]
By the definition of \(b_i\), equation (8) says
\[
a_{3773+K+1}+1\equiv1\pmod p,
\qquad
a_{3773+K}+1\equiv1\pmod p.
\]
Equivalently,
\[
p\mid a_{K+3774}
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
p\mid a_{K+3773}. \tag{9}
\]

Let
\[
x=a_{K+3774}=a_{N-1},
\qquad y=a_{K+3773}=a_{N-2},
\qquad g=\gcd(x,y).
\]
Both \(x\) and \(y\) are positive. Indeed, their indices are at least 3775, so the assumed identity (1) expresses each as 1 plus two nonnegative integers. From (9), \(p\) divides both \(x\) and \(y\), hence
\[
p\mid g.
\]
Since \(g>0\) and \(p=195318521017\geq2\), it follows that
\[
g\geq p\geq2. \tag{10}
\]
Notice that no assertion that \(p\) is prime is needed: any common divisor \(p>1\) is enough.

We now compare the actual defining recurrence at index \(N\) with the conjectured formula there. The defining recurrence gives
\[
a_N=g+\frac{x+y}{g}. \tag{11}
\]
On the other hand, because \(N\geq3775\), the assumed identity (1) gives
\[
a_N=1+x+y. \tag{12}
\]
These two values cannot be equal when \(x,y>0\) and \(g=\gcd(x,y)\geq2\). Here is the elementary inequality in detail. Since \(g\mid x\) and \(g\mid y\), write
\[
x+y=qg
\]
for an integer \(q\). Positivity of \(x,y\), together with \(g\mid x,y\), implies \(x\geq g\) and \(y\geq g\), so \(q\geq2\). Therefore
\[
\begin{aligned}
(1+x+y)-\left(g+\frac{x+y}{g}\right)
 &=1+qg-g-q\\
 &=(g-1)(q-1).
\end{aligned}
\]
Because both \(g\) and \(q\) are at least 2, this difference is at least 1. Thus
\[
g+\frac{x+y}{g}<1+x+y, \tag{13}
\]
contradicting the simultaneous equalities (11) and (12).

The contradiction arose from assuming that the conjecture holds for every \(n\geq3775\). More concretely, under that assumption the two terms immediately preceding
\[
N=249580077008
\]
would both be divisible by \(195318521017\), forcing their gcd to exceed 1; at index \(N\), the original gcd recurrence would then give a value strictly smaller than \(1+a_{N-1}+a_{N-2}\). Hence the first claimed formula fails somewhere no later than this forced contradiction (and in particular the universal conjunction of the three claimed formulas is false). This disproves the OEIS conjecture.
